qaraqara-charka-confederation.t: A confederation of Aymara-speaking peoples in the southern Bolivian highlands, renowned as warriors and later linked to the silver mines of Potosí.
qaraqara-charka-confederation.o: In the centuries after Tiwanaku's collapse, the Qaraqara and Charka formed a federation of peoples in the southern highlands of modern [[s:republic-of-bolivia|Bolivia]], around [[e:potosi|Potosí]] and [[e:sucre|Chuquisaca]], around 1200. The federation included groups such as the Chuy and Chicha.
qaraqara-charka-confederation.r: The confederation was organised in two halves led by the Qaraqara in the south and the Charka in the north, each under hereditary lords. It is known chiefly from a memorial written by its lords in 1582, which describes their service as soldiers for the [[e:inca-empire|Incas]]. The peoples herded llamas, farmed tubers and [[e:maize|maize]], and worked [[e:silver|silver]] and other metals.
qaraqara-charka-confederation.e: The confederation came under [[e:inca-empire|Inca]] rule around 1460 and served the Incas in war. After the Spanish conquest, its lands formed the core of the [[s:royal-audiencia-of-charcas|Royal Audiencia of Charcas]], and the [[e:silver|silver]] mountain of [[e:potosi|Potosí]], discovered in 1545, lay in Qaraqara territory.

qajar-iran.t: The Turkmen-origin dynasty that ruled Iran from Tehran through its loss of the Caucasus, Great Power rivalry and the Constitutional Revolution of 1906.
qajar-iran.o: [[e:agha-mohammad-khan-qajar|Agha Mohammad Khan]], chief of the [[e:qajar-dynasty|Qajar]] tribe, fought the [[e:zand-dynasty|Zand dynasty]] after [[e:karim-khan-zand|Karim Khan's]] death in 1779. He made [[e:tehran|Tehran]] his capital in 1786, defeated the last Zand ruler [[e:lotf-ali-khan|Lotf Ali Khan]] in 1794, sacked [[e:tbilisi|Tiflis]] in 1795 and was crowned shah in 1796. He was assassinated in 1797, and his nephew [[e:fath-ali-shah-qajar|Fath Ali Shah]] succeeded.
qajar-iran.r: [[e:fath-ali-shah-qajar|Fath Ali Shah]] lost the [[e:caucasus|Caucasus]] to the [[s:russian-empire|Russian Empire]] by the treaties of Gulistan (1813) and [[e:treaty-of-turkmenchay|Turkmenchay]] (1828). Under [[e:naser-al-din-shah-qajar|Naser al-Din Shah]] (1848 to 1896) the minister [[e:amir-kabir|Amir Kabir]] founded the [[e:dar-ul-funun|Dar ol-Fonun]] college, but the shahs relied on foreign loans and concessions, provoking the tobacco protest of 1891 to 1892. The [[e:persian-constitutional-revolution|Constitutional Revolution]] created a parliament ([[e:national-consultative-assembly|Majlis]]) in 1906, while the [[e:anglo-russian-convention|Anglo-Russian Convention]] of 1907 divided [[e:iran|Iran]] into spheres of influence.
qajar-iran.e: After occupation in the [[e:first-world-war|First World War]], [[e:reza-shah|Reza Khan]] seized power in a 1921 coup. In 1925 the [[e:national-consultative-assembly|Majlis]] deposed [[e:ahmad-shah-qajar|Ahmad Shah]], ending the dynasty, and a constituent assembly made Reza Khan shah, founding [[s:pahlavi-iran|Pahlavi Iran]].

qi-1130-1137.t: A Jurchen client state in Henan and Shaanxi under the former Song official Liu Yu, used as a buffer and spearhead against the Southern Song.
qi-1130-1137.o: [[e:liu-yu-qi|Liu Yu]], [[e:song-dynasty|Song]] prefect of Jinan, surrendered to the [[e:jurchens|Jurchen]] in 1128. In 1130 the [[s:jin-dynasty-1115-1234|Jin dynasty]] (1115-1234) installed him as emperor of [[s:qi-huang-chao|Great Qi]] to govern the conquered lands south of the [[e:yellow-river|Yellow River]], first from Daming and from 1132 from [[e:kaifeng|Kaifeng]].
qi-1130-1137.r: [[e:liu-yu-qi|Liu Yu]] ruled with Chinese-style institutions but imposed heavy taxes and labour to pay for war. With Jin support his armies attacked [[s:southern-song|Southern Song]] several times between 1133 and 1136, but were defeated by [[e:song-dynasty|Song]] generals including [[e:yue-fei|Yue Fei]], and Qi lost credibility with its masters.
qi-1130-1137.e: In 1137 the Jin court abolished Qi, demoted [[e:liu-yu-qi|Liu Yu]] to a prince and took the territory under direct rule. Its lands were briefly returned to the [[e:song-dynasty|Song]] in a treaty of 1139 before the [[e:jurchens|Jurchen]] reoccupied them in 1140.

qwabe-chiefdom.t: A northern Nguni chiefdom, senior kin of the Zulu, that was conquered and absorbed by Shaka around 1818.
qwabe-chiefdom.o: Tradition holds that Qwabe and [[e:zulu-kingdom|Zulu]] were sons of Malandela, and the Qwabe line was originally the larger and more senior. By the 18th century the Qwabe were settled near the lower [[e:mhlathuze-river|Mhlathuze]] river in what is now [[e:kwazulu-natal|KwaZulu-Natal]].
qwabe-chiefdom.r: Qwabe chiefs ruled [[e:cattle|cattle]]-herding homesteads through royal kin and councillors, and their lineage claimed ritual seniority over the [[e:zulu-kingdom|Zulu]]. Under Kondlo and later Phakathwayo, the chiefdom was among the significant powers south of the [[s:mthethwa-paramountcy|Mthethwa Paramountcy]].
qwabe-chiefdom.e: Around 1818 [[e:shaka-zulu-king|Shaka]] defeated Phakathwayo, who died soon after, and the Qwabe were incorporated into the [[s:zulu-kingdom|Zulu Kingdom]], providing many of its soldiers and notables. Some Qwabe later broke away under Nqetho in 1829.

que.t: Que, a Neo-Hittite kingdom of the Cilician plain around Adana, known for its horses and for bilingual inscriptions in Luwian and Phoenician.
que.o: After the Hittite collapse, a kingdom arose in the fertile Cilician plain, formerly [[s:kizzuwatna|Kizzuwatna]]. Its people called it Hiyawa, a name some link with the Greek [[s:ahhiyawa|Ahhiyawa]], and its capital was [[e:adana|Adana]]. Assyrian texts call it Que from the 9th century BCE.
que.r: Kings such as [[e:awariku|Awariku]], the Urikki of Assyrian texts, ruled with Phoenician as a prestige language beside Luwian; bilingual inscriptions at [[e:karatepe|Karatepe]] and [[e:cinekoy-inscription|Çineköy]] are key to deciphering Luwian hieroglyphs. Que bred horses, which the Bible says [[e:solomon|Solomon]] bought there.
que.e: [[e:shalmaneser-iii|Shalmaneser III]] of the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]] campaigned against King Kate. [[e:awariku|Urikki]] became a [[e:vassal|vassal]] of Tiglath-Pileser III, and by 713 BCE [[e:sargon-ii|Sargon II]] had made Que an Assyrian province.

quaiti-sultanate.t: The richest of the Hadrami sultanates, founded with money earned in Indian service and ruled from the port of Mukalla.
quaiti-sultanate.o: The Qu'aiti were a [[e:yafa|Yafa]]'i family whose head, [[e:umar-ibn-awad-al-quaiti|Umar ibn Awad al-Qu'aiti]], rose to high rank as a commander in the army of the [[e:nizam-of-hyderabad|Nizam of Hyderabad]]. With Indian wealth they bought land and influence in [[s:kingdom-of-hadramawt|Hadramawt]], taking [[e:shibam|Shibam]] and the port of [[e:ash-shihr|Shihr]] from around 1858, then [[e:mukalla|Mukalla]] from the [[s:kasadi-sultanate|Kasadi Sultanate]] in 1881.
quaiti-sultanate.r: [[e:mukalla|Mukalla]] became the capital, with a palace, customs house and modern administration; the sultans long spent much time in [[e:hyderabad-sindh|Hyderabad]]. Treaties with [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] from 1882 made the state part of the [[s:aden-protectorate|Aden Protectorate]], later the Eastern [[e:aden-protectorate|Aden Protectorate]], and the Kathiri-Qu'aiti agreement of 1918 settled relations with the [[s:kathiri-sultanate|Kathiri Sultanate]]. Remittances from [[e:southeast-asia|Southeast Asia]] and the [[e:hadhrami-bedouin-legion|Hadhrami Bedouin Legion]] sustained the state.
quaiti-sultanate.e: In September 1967 the [[e:national-liberation-front-south-yemen|National Liberation Front]] seized [[e:mukalla|Mukalla]] while the young sultan [[e:ghalib-ibn-awad-al-quaiti|Ghalib ibn Awad al-Qu'aiti]] was abroad, and the sultanate was abolished within [[s:south-yemen|South Yemen]].

qin-xue-ju.t: A short-lived rebel empire in Gansu whose armies briefly beat the young Tang but were destroyed by Li Shimin in 618.
qin-xue-ju.o: [[e:xue-ju|Xue Ju]], a rich and powerful man of [[e:lanzhou|Jincheng]] (modern Lanzhou), rose in revolt in 617 as the [[s:sui-dynasty|Sui Dynasty]] disintegrated. He took the title Hegemon-King of [[s:western-qin|Western Qin]], then proclaimed himself emperor of [[e:qin-dynasty|Qin]] and moved his capital east to [[e:tianshui|Tianshui]], threatening the Wei valley around [[e:changan|Chang'an]].
qin-xue-ju.r: The regime was essentially a military confederation of [[e:gansu|Gansu]] frontier troops, known for their harsh treatment of captives, and [[e:xue-ju|Xue Ju]] appointed relatives and generals to the main offices rather than building a civil administration. Its aim was to take [[e:changan|Chang'an]] itself. In 618 its army defeated [[s:later-tang|Tang]] forces under [[e:emperor-taizong-of-tang|Li Shimin]] at [[e:battle-of-qianshuiyuan|Qianshuiyuan]], when Li Shimin was ill.
qin-xue-ju.e: [[e:xue-ju|Xue Ju]] died soon after this victory, and his son [[e:xue-rengao|Xue Rengao]] succeeded him. Later in 618 [[e:emperor-taizong-of-tang|Li Shimin]] returned, wore down the [[e:qin-dynasty|Qin]] army and routed it at [[e:battle-of-qianshuiyuan|Qianshuiyuan]]; Xue Rengao surrendered and was executed in [[e:changan|Chang'an]], opening the north-west to the [[s:tang-dynasty|Tang Dynasty]].

qasimid-state.t: The Zaydi imamate that drove the Ottomans out of Yemen in 1636 and briefly united the country while Mocha coffee reached Europe.
qasimid-state.o: In 1597 [[e:al-qasim-ibn-muhammad|al-Qasim ibn Muhammad]], a Zaydi scholar, proclaimed himself [[e:imam|imam]] and began a revolt against [[s:yemen-eyalet|Yemen Eyalet]] from the northern mountains. His son [[e:al-muayyad-muhammad|al-Mu'ayyad Muhammad]] continued the war until the [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]] evacuated [[s:republic-of-yemen|Yemen]] in 1636, leaving the Qasimid family masters of the country.
qasimid-state.r: Under [[e:al-mutawakkil-ismail|al-Mutawakkil Isma'il]], [[e:imam|imam]] from 1644 to 1676, the state reached its greatest extent, taking [[e:aden|Aden]], [[s:sultanate-of-lahej|Lahej]] and [[s:kingdom-of-hadramawt|Hadramawt]]. Its wealth came from [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]], shipped through [[s:mohu|Mocha]] to [[e:cairo|Cairo]] and, through [[e:dutch|Dutch]], English and French factories, to [[e:europe|Europe]]. Although Zaydi doctrine called for elected imams, succession became dynastic, and the court at Sanaa or al-Mawahib resembled a monarchy.
qasimid-state.e: From the early 18th century southern and eastern districts broke away, including the [[s:sultanate-of-lahej|Sultanate of Lahej]], and [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]] exports fell as colonial plantations grew. Rival [[e:imam|imams]], tribal revolts and Wahhabi raids weakened it further. In 1872 the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] took Sanaa and formed the [[s:yemen-vilayet|Yemen Vilayet]].

qara-qoyunlu.t: A Turkmen confederation, the 'Black Sheep', that ruled Azerbaijan, Iraq and much of Iran in the 15th century until defeated by the rival White Sheep.
qara-qoyunlu.o: The Qara Qoyunlu were [[e:oghuz-turks|Oghuz]] [[e:turkmen|Turkmen]] tribes of the region around [[e:lake-van|Lake Van]] and [[e:mosul|Mosul]]. Their leader [[e:bayram-khwaja|Bayram Khwaja]] emerged in the 1370s as a [[e:vassal|vassal]] of the [[s:jalayirids|Jalayirids]]. [[e:qara-yusuf|Qara Yusuf]] fought [[e:timur|Timur]], fled to the [[s:mamluk-sultanate|Mamluk Sultanate]], returned after Timur's death and in 1410 defeated and killed [[e:ahmad-jalayir|Ahmad Jalayir]], taking [[e:tabriz|Tabriz]] and [[e:baghdad|Baghdad]].
qara-qoyunlu.r: The confederation was ruled by the [[e:qara-yusuf|Qara Yusuf]] family through tribal leaders and Persian officials, with [[e:tabriz|Tabriz]] as capital. [[e:qara-iskander|Iskandar]] fought the [[e:timurid-empire|Timurid]] [[e:shah-rukh|Shah Rukh]]. [[e:jahan-shah-qara-qoyunlu|Jahan Shah]] (1438 to 1467) expanded the state to its greatest extent, briefly taking [[e:herat|Herat]] in 1458, and wrote poetry in Turkic and Persian; the [[e:blue-mosque-of-tabriz|Blue Mosque of Tabriz]] was built in his reign. The dynasty has been associated with Shia sympathies, though this is debated.
qara-qoyunlu.e: In 1467 [[e:uzun-hasan|Uzun Hasan]] of the [[s:aq-qoyunlu|Aq Qoyunlu]] defeated and killed [[e:jahan-shah-qara-qoyunlu|Jahan Shah]]. His son Hasan Ali was defeated in 1468, and [[e:aq-qoyunlu|Aq Qoyunlu]] absorbed the state.

qutlugh-khanid-dynasty.t: A dynasty of Qara Khitai origin that ruled Kerman under Mongol overlordship and produced two notable women rulers.
qutlugh-khanid-dynasty.o: [[e:baraq-hajib|Baraq Hajib]], an officer of [[s:qara-khitai|Qara Khitai]] origin who had served the [[s:khwarazmian-empire|Khwarazmian Empire]], seized [[e:kerman|Kerman]] in 1222 during the chaos of the Mongol invasions. He submitted to the [[e:mongols|Mongols]] and received the title Qutlugh Khan, which gave the dynasty its name.
qutlugh-khanid-dynasty.r: The Qutlugh-Khanids ruled [[e:kerman|Kerman]] as [[e:vassal|vassals]] first of the [[e:great-khan|Great Khans]] and then of the [[s:ilkhanate|Ilkhanate]], keeping the province prosperous through trade with the Gulf. [[e:qutlugh-terken-khatun|Qutlugh Terken Khatun]], widow of Qutb al-Din Muhammad, governed from 1257 to 1282 and was remembered for justice, irrigation works and building. Her daughter [[e:padishah-khatun|Padishah Khatun]], wife successively of the [[e:ilkhan|Ilkhans]] [[e:abaqa-khan|Abaqa]] and [[e:gaykhatu|Gaykhatu]], ruled Kerman from 1292 but was executed in 1295.
qutlugh-khanid-dynasty.e: Family rivalries and Ilkhanid intervention weakened the dynasty. In 1306 the [[e:ilkhan|Ilkhan]] [[e:oljeitu|Öljeitü]] ended its rule and placed [[e:kerman|Kerman]] under appointed governors.

qi-206-bc.t: The revived kingdom of Qi in Shandong, fought over by the Tian clan, Xiang Yu and Han Xin during the Chu-Han war, until Han Xin made himself its king in 203 BCE.
qi-206-bc.o: In 206 BCE [[e:xiang-yu|Xiang Yu]] split the old [[s:state-of-qi|State of Qi]] into three, making the Qi general [[e:tian-du|Tian Du]] King of Qi at [[e:linzi|Linzi]]. [[e:tian-rong|Tian Rong]], the clan strongman left out of the settlement, drove [[e:tian|Tian]] Du out within months, killed the kings of Jiaodong and Jibei, and made himself king of a reunited Qi.
qi-206-bc.r: Qi became the main distraction that kept [[e:xiang-yu|Xiang Yu]] from crushing [[e:liu-bang|Liu Bang]]. Xiang Yu invaded in 205 BCE and [[e:tian-rong|Tian Rong]] was killed, but [[e:tian-heng|Tian Heng]] rallied resistance and installed [[e:tian|Tian]] [[e:rong-people|Rong's]] son [[e:tian-guang|Tian Guang]] as king, with himself as chancellor. The kingdom rested on the loyalty of the Tian clan and the wealth of the [[e:shandong|Shandong]] coast.
qi-206-bc.e: In 203 BCE, as [[e:liu-bang|Liu Bang's]] envoy [[e:li-yiji|Li Yiji]] negotiated Qi's submission, [[e:han-xin|Han Xin]] attacked anyway, routed the relief army of [[e:long-ju|Long Ju]] on the [[e:wei-river-shandong|Wei River]] and captured [[e:tian-guang|Tian Guang]]. Han Xin became King of Qi. [[e:tian-heng|Tian Heng]] later fled to an island; summoned by Liu Bang in 202 BCE, he killed himself rather than submit, and his followers on the island did the same.

qedarites.t: The most powerful Arab tribal confederation of the first millennium BCE, controlling desert routes from Syria to the oases of north Arabia.
qedarites.o: The Qedarites (biblical Kedar) appear in Assyrian records from the 8th century BCE as [[e:camel|camel]]-herding [[e:arabs|Arabs]] of the Syrian desert and northern [[e:arabia|Arabia]]. Their centre was the oasis of [[e:dumat-al-jandal|Adummatu]], modern Dumat al-Jandal, which held the shrine of their gods. Queen [[e:zabibe|Zabibe]] paid tribute to Tiglath-Pileser III in 738 BCE, followed by Queen [[e:samsi|Samsi]].
qedarites.r: They were led by kings and, unusually, by queens who also served as priestesses, among them [[e:teelhunu|Te'elhunu]]. The confederation controlled [[e:caravan-trade|caravan routes]] carrying [[e:incense|incense]] from south [[e:arabia|Arabia]] to the [[e:levant|Levant]] and supplied [[e:camel|camels]] and guides to imperial armies. Repeated revolts brought punitive campaigns: [[e:sennacherib|Sennacherib]] seized their idols, and [[e:ashurbanipal|Ashurbanipal]] fought [[e:yauta|Yauta]] son of [[e:hazael-of-qedar|Hazael]] in the 7th century BCE.
qedarites.e: Under the [[s:achaemenid-empire|Achaemenid Empire]] the Qedarites kept their autonomy; [[e:geshem-the-arab|Geshem the Arab]], opponent of [[e:nehemiah|Nehemiah]], and his son Qaynu, named king of Qedar on a [[e:silver|silver]] bowl from [[e:egypt|Egypt]], date to the 5th century BCE. By the 3rd century BCE their place was taken by the [[s:nabataean-kingdom|Nabataean Kingdom]].

qashqai-confederation.t: A Turkic-speaking confederation of nomadic tribes in Fars whose ilkhans were a major political force in southern Iran until exiled in 1954.
qashqai-confederation.o: The Qashqai are Turkic tribes who migrate seasonally between winter pastures near the Gulf and summer pastures in the [[e:zagros-mountains|Zagros]] north of [[e:shiraz|Shiraz]]. They coalesced as a confederation in the 18th century, and under [[e:karim-khan-zand|Karim Khan]] of the [[s:zand-empire|Zand Empire]] their chief Jani Agha rose to prominence. [[e:fath-ali-shah-qajar|Fath Ali Shah]] of [[s:qajar-iran|Qajar Iran]] recognised his son [[e:jani-khan-qashqai|Jani Khan]] as ilkhan in 1818.
qashqai-confederation.r: The ilkhans ruled through tribal khans and kalantars, controlling migration routes, taxes and armed horsemen. Qashqai women are known for weaving gabbeh rugs and kilims. In the [[e:first-world-war|First World War]] [[e:ismail-khan-qashqai|Ismail Khan]] Solat al-Dowleh fought the British-led [[e:south-persia-rifles|South Persia Rifles]]. [[e:reza-shah|Reza Shah]] forced the tribes to settle and Solat al-Dowleh died in prison in 1933.
qashqai-confederation.e: After 1941 his sons Naser Khan and Khosrow Khan revived Qashqai power and supported [[e:mohammad-mosaddegh|Mohammad Mosaddegh]]. After the 1953 coup they were exiled in 1954, ending the confederation's political autonomy; the Qashqai people remain a distinct community.

quirigua.t: A small Maya kingdom in the Motagua valley that won independence from Copán in 738 and raised the tallest carved stone monuments of the Maya world.
quirigua.o: Quiriguá was founded or refounded in 426 CE as a dependency of [[s:copan|Copán]], about 50 kilometres to the south, by agents of Copán's founder [[e:kinich-yax-kuk-mo|K'inich Yax K'uk' Mo']]. It controlled the lower [[e:motagua-river|Motagua]] river, a route for jade and obsidian toward the [[e:caribbean|Caribbean]].
quirigua.r: Its ruler [[e:kak-tiliw-chan-yopaat|K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat]] was installed under Copán's authority in 724. In 738, probably backed by the [[s:kingdom-of-kaan|Kingdom of Kaan]], he captured and beheaded Copán's king [[e:waxaklajuun-ubaah-kawiil|Waxaklajuun Ub'aah K'awiil]], freeing Quiriguá. He celebrated with enormous sandstone stelae, including Stela E, over 10 metres tall, and zoomorphic boulders carved with long texts.
quirigua.e: Quiriguá prospered for several decades after its victory but its last monuments date to about 810, after which it declined. It was declared a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] in 1981.

qi-huang-chao.t: The regime of the rebel Huang Chao, who seized Chang'an and declared himself emperor of Great Qi, dealing the Tang dynasty a blow from which it never recovered.
qi-huang-chao.o: [[e:huang-chao|Huang Chao]], a salt smuggler who had failed the civil service examinations, joined [[e:wang-xianzhi|Wang Xianzhi's]] rebellion in 875 and led it after Wang's death in 878. His army swept through southern [[e:china|China]], sacking [[e:guangzhou|Guangzhou]] in 879, then turned north, took [[e:luoyang|Luoyang]] and entered [[e:changan|Chang'an]] at the start of 881, proclaiming himself emperor of Great Qi.
qi-huang-chao.r: [[e:huang-chao|Huang Chao]] set up a court with officials, reign titles and some surrendered [[s:later-tang|Tang]] servants, while [[e:emperor-xizong-of-tang|Emperor Xizong]] fled to [[e:chengdu|Chengdu]]. But the regime controlled little beyond the capital region, food ran short, and executions of officials and massacres of the city's population turned the elite against it.
qi-huang-chao.e: His general [[e:zhu-wen|Zhu Wen]] defected to the [[s:later-tang|Tang]] in 882, and in 883 the [[e:shatuo|Shatuo]] cavalry of [[e:li-keyong|Li Keyong]] drove [[e:huang-chao|Huang Chao]] from [[e:changan|Chang'an]]. He fled east and was killed in 884 near [[e:mount-tai|Mount Tai]]. The [[s:tang-dynasty|Tang Dynasty]] survived only in name, as Zhu Wen and Li Keyong became the dominant warlords.

qasim-khanate.t: A Tatar vassal state created by Moscow on the Oka, whose Muslim khans served the Russian rulers for over two centuries.
qasim-khanate.o: In 1452 [[e:vasily-ii-of-moscow|Vasily II of Moscow]] granted the town of [[e:kasimov|Gorodets Meshchersky]] on the [[e:oka-river|Oka]], later renamed Kasimov, to Qasim, a son of [[e:ulugh-muhammad|Ulugh Muhammad]], founder of the [[s:khanate-of-kazan|Khanate of Kazan]], who had entered [[e:moscow|Moscow's]] service. It became a small [[e:tatars|Tatar]] khanate under Moscow's protection.
qasim-khanate.r: Its khans, descendants of [[e:genghis-khan|Genghis Khan]], ruled a [[e:tatars|Tatar]] nobility and local [[e:meshchera|Meshchera]] and Russian subjects, kept their Muslim faith and served in [[e:moscow|Moscow's]] armies. Moscow used them as rival candidates for the throne of [[e:kazan|Kazan]], and [[e:shah-ali-khan|Shah Ali]] of [[e:kasimov|Kasimov]] was installed there more than once. The khan's mosque and the tomb of Shah Ali still stand in Kasimov.
qasim-khanate.e: The khanate gradually lost its independence, and its later rulers converted to [[e:christianity|Christianity]] or were controlled by [[e:moscow|Moscow]]. After the death of the last ruler, [[e:fatima-soltan|Fatima Sultan]], in 1681, it was abolished and absorbed into the [[s:tsardom-of-russia|Tsardom of Russia]].

qaraunas.t: A Mongol military confederation of the Afghan borderlands, raiders of India and Persia who became kingmakers in the Chagatai lands.
qaraunas.o: The Qara'unas originated in Mongol garrison troops stationed in what is now [[s:islamic-emirate-of-afghanistan-2021-present|Afghanistan]] in the mid-13th century, including contingents left by the general [[e:neguder|Negüder]], after whom they were also called Negüderis. By the 1260s they formed an independent force in the region of [[e:ghazni|Ghazni]] and [[e:balkh|Balkh]].
qaraunas.r: They were a nomadic warrior confederation of mixed Mongol and Turkic origin, organised in [[e:tumen|tumens]] under their own commanders. They raided the [[s:ilkhanate|Ilkhanate]], [[e:kerman|Kerman]] and [[e:fars|Fars]], and launched repeated invasions of the [[s:delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]] in the late 13th and early 14th centuries. They later formed a major component of the [[e:chagatai-khanate|Chagatai Khanate's]] western forces.
qaraunas.e: Their leader [[e:qazaghan|Qazaghan]] dominated the [[s:western-chagatai-khanate|Western Chagatai Khanate]] from 1346 until his murder in 1358. His grandson [[e:amir-husayn|Amir Husayn]] was overthrown by [[e:timur|Timur]] in 1370, and the Qara'unas were absorbed into the [[e:timurid-empire|Timurid]] army.

quadi.t: A Suebian people north of the middle Danube who, with the Marcomanni, fought Rome under Marcus Aurelius and later joined the great migration into Spain.
quadi.o: The Quadi settled in [[s:great-moravia|Moravia]] and western [[e:slovakia|Slovakia]], probably moving there from the Main region around the same time as the [[s:marcomanni|Marcomanni]] at the end of the 1st century BCE. They formed part of the realm of [[e:maroboduus|Maroboduus]] and later of the client kingdom of [[e:vannius|Vannius]], established by [[e:rome|Rome]] in 19.
quadi.r: Ruled by kings, often confirmed by [[e:rome|Rome]], the Quadi lived in villages, traded with Roman [[e:pannonia|Pannonia]] and buried their elite with Roman imports. They joined the [[e:marcomannic-wars|Marcomannic Wars]] from 166; the 'Rain Miracle' depicted on the Column of [[e:marcus-aurelius|Marcus Aurelius]] took place on their territory. Rome built forward posts in their land such as [[e:musov|Mušov]].
quadi.e: In 374 the killing of their king [[e:gabinius-king-of-the-quadi|Gabinius]] by a Roman officer provoked a raid into [[e:pannonia|Pannonia]], and Emperor [[e:valentinian-i|Valentinian I]] died in 375 while confronting their envoys. In 406 many Quadi crossed the [[e:rhine|Rhine]] with the [[e:vandals|Vandals]] and [[s:alans|Alans]], probably becoming part of the Suebian kingdom in [[e:spain|Spain]].

qatna.t: Qatna, a wealthy Bronze Age kingdom near Homs whose intact royal tomb and palace show Syria's prosperity between Egypt, Mitanni and the Hittites.
qatna.o: Qatna, at Tell el-Mishrifeh, was refounded at the start of the 2nd millennium BCE inside huge square earthen ramparts. Its Amorite kings controlled central [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]] and the [[e:caravan-trade|caravan routes]] from the [[e:euphrates|Euphrates]] to the coast, and became the main rivals of [[s:yamhad|Yamhad]].
qatna.r: In the [[s:mari|Mari]] era King [[e:ishhi-addu|Ishhi-Addu]] allied with [[e:shamshi-adad-i|Shamshi-Adad]] and married his daughter to [[e:yasmah-addu|Yasmah-Addu]]. The royal palace held a hypogeum, found unplundered in 2002, with gold, [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and the bones of generations of the royal family. Later kings left Akkadian archives with many Hurrian words.
qatna.e: In the 14th century BCE Qatna lay between the [[s:mitanni-empire|Mitanni Empire]], the [[s:egyptian-empire-new-kingdom|Egyptian Empire New Kingdom]] and the [[s:hittite-empire|Hittite Empire]]. Its king Akizzi appealed to [[e:egypt|Egypt]] in the [[e:amarna-letters|Amarna letters]], but Hittite forces under [[e:suppiluliuma-i|Suppiluliuma I]] sacked the city c. 1340 BCE and it never recovered.

qin-dynasty.t: China's first imperial dynasty, which unified the warring states in 221 BCE and imposed one script, one currency and one bureaucracy, then collapsed within fifteen years.
qin-dynasty.o: Between 230 and 221 BCE King [[s:state-of-zheng|Zheng]] of the [[s:state-of-qin|State of Qin]] conquered the six rival states, the last being the [[s:state-of-qi|State of Qi]]. He took the new title Huangdi, emperor, and is known as [[e:qin-shi-huang|Qin Shi Huang]], the First Emperor. His capital remained [[e:xianyang|Xianyang]] in the Wei valley.
qin-dynasty.r: Advised by [[e:li-si|Li Si]], the emperor abolished hereditary fiefs and divided the empire into 36, later more, [[e:commandery|commanderies]] run by appointed officials. Script, weights, measures, coinage and axle widths were standardised, roads and the [[e:lingqu|Lingqu]] canal were built, and [[e:meng-tian|Meng Tian]] linked earlier walls against the [[e:xiongnu-empire|Xiongnu]]. Harsh Legalist law, mass labour levies and the burning of books in 213 BCE bred resentment. The emperor's mausoleum was guarded by the Terracotta Army.
qin-dynasty.e: After the [[e:qin-shi-huang|First Emperor]] died in 210 BCE, Zhao [[e:gao|Gao]] and [[e:li-si|Li Si]] installed his son [[e:qin-er-shi|Huhai]] as Second Emperor. Revolts led by [[e:chen-sheng|Chen Sheng]] began in 209 BCE, and in 206 BCE the last ruler, [[e:ziying|Ziying]], surrendered to [[e:liu-bang|Liu Bang]]. The [[s:han-dynasty|Han Dynasty]] kept the Qin system of centralised imperial government.

qi-five-dynasties.t: The domain of the warlord Li Maozhen west of Chang'an, which stayed loyal to the memory of the Tang and refused to recognise the Later Liang.
qi-five-dynasties.o: [[e:li-maozhen|Li Maozhen]], born [[e:song-dynasty|Song]] Wentong, rose as an officer in the imperial guard and became military governor of [[e:fengxiang|Fengxiang]], west of [[e:changan|Chang'an]], in 887, receiving the imperial surname Li. He was made Prince of Qi in 901 and that year took [[e:emperor-zhaozong-of-tang|Emperor Zhaozong]] into his custody until [[e:zhu-wen|Zhu Wen's]] siege of Fengxiang forced him to hand him over in 903.
qi-five-dynasties.r: After the [[s:later-tang|Tang]] fell in 907, [[e:li-maozhen|Li Maozhen]] kept using the Tang reign era and the title Prince of Qi but never declared himself emperor. He ran a princely court with appointed officials. His domain shrank steadily as [[s:former-shu|Former Shu]] took his southern prefectures, and he relied on alliances with the state of [[s:jin-five-dynasties|Jin (Five Dynasties)]].
qi-five-dynasties.e: When [[e:li-cunxu|Li Cunxu]] destroyed the [[s:later-liang|Later Liang]] and founded the [[s:later-tang|Later Tang]], [[e:li-maozhen|Li Maozhen]] submitted in 924 and was confirmed as Prince of [[e:qin-dynasty|Qin]]. He died later that year, and his son Li Congyan succeeded him only as an ordinary provincial governor.

qara-khitai.t: A Khitan empire founded in Central Asia by refugees from the fallen Liao dynasty, whose defeat of the Seljuks inspired European legends of Prester John.
qara-khitai.o: When the [[e:jurchens|Jurchen]] destroyed the Khitan [[s:liao-dynasty|Liao dynasty]] in northern [[e:china|China]] in 1125, the prince [[e:yelu-dashi|Yelü Dashi]] fled west with followers. He took [[e:balasagun|Balasagun]] from the [[s:eastern-kara-khanid-khanate|Eastern Kara-Khanid Khanate]] around 1134, proclaimed himself gurkhan and founded the Western [[e:liao-dynasty|Liao]], known as Qara Khitai.
qara-khitai.r: The gurkhans ruled a mostly Muslim population through [[e:vassal|vassal]] dynasties such as the [[e:kara-khanid-khanate|Kara-Khanids]], the [[s:kingdom-of-qocho|Kingdom of Qocho]] and the [[e:khwarazmian-empire|Khwarazmshahs]], collecting tribute instead of governing directly. The court kept Chinese-style titles and reign names while tolerating all religions. In 1141 [[e:yelu-dashi|Yelü Dashi]] crushed the Seljuk sultan [[e:ahmad-sanjar|Ahmad Sanjar]] at the Qatwan steppe near [[e:samarkand|Samarkand]], news of which reached [[e:europe|Europe]] as the legend of [[e:prester-john|Prester John]].
qara-khitai.e: In 1211 the Naiman prince [[e:kuchlug|Kuchlug]], a refugee from [[e:genghis-khan|Genghis Khan]], seized the throne, persecuting Muslims. The [[s:khwarazmian-empire|Khwarazmian Empire]] took its western lands, and in 1218 Mongol forces under [[e:jebe|Jebe]] killed Kuchlug and absorbed Qara Khitai.
qara-khitai.re: Buddhism, Sunni Islam, Church of the East

qarmatians-of-bahrain.t: A radical Isma'ili state in eastern Arabia, ruled by a council at al-Ahsa, that stole the Black Stone from Mecca in 930.
qarmatians-of-bahrain.o: In 899 the missionary [[e:abu-said-al-jannabi|Abu Sa'id al-Jannabi]], preaching the coming of the [[e:mahdi|Mahdi]], won over [[e:bedouin|Bedouin]] and peasants in eastern [[e:arabia|Arabia]], then called [[s:sheikhdom-of-bahrain|Bahrain]], and took [[e:al-ahsa-oasis|al-Ahsa]] and [[e:qatif|Qatif]]. His state broke with the [[e:fatimid-caliphate|Fatimid Caliphate's]] claims to leadership and became a separate Qarmatian power.
qarmatians-of-bahrain.r: After [[e:abu-said-al-jannabi|Abu Sa'id]], the state was governed by a council of his descendants and leading men. Visitors such as [[e:nasir-khusraw|Nasir Khusraw]] reported that citizens paid no taxes, debts were interest free and thousands of African slaves worked the date groves. Under [[e:abu-tahir-al-jannabi|Abu Tahir]] the [[e:qarmatians|Qarmatians]] raided [[e:basra|Basra]] and [[e:kufa|Kufa]], attacked pilgrim caravans and in 930 sacked [[e:mecca|Mecca]], carrying the [[e:black-stone|Black Stone]] to [[e:al-ahsa-oasis|al-Ahsa]] until 951.
qarmatians-of-bahrain.e: Their power declined after defeats by the [[e:fatimid-caliphate|Fatimids]] and the [[s:buyid-dynasty|Buyids]] and the loss of [[e:oman|Oman]]. In 1077 [[e:abd-allah-al-uyuni|Abd Allah al-Uyuni]], a local chief, overthrew them with help from the [[s:seljuk-empire|Seljuk Empire]] and founded the [[s:uyunid-emirate|Uyunid Emirate]].

quitu-cara.t: The peoples of the Quito basin before the Incas, remembered in Ecuadorian tradition as the Kingdom of Quito ruled by the Shyris, a story many historians doubt.
quitu-cara.o: The Quitu were the inhabitants of the highland basin where [[e:quito|Quito]] now stands, settled since at least the first millennium CE. In 1789 the [[e:jesuits|Jesuit]] historian [[e:juan-de-velasco|Juan de Velasco]] wrote that the Cara people came from the coast around 980 and founded a kingdom ruled by kings called Shyris, which united the northern highlands.
quitu-cara.r: Archaeology shows a landscape of local chiefdoms around [[e:quito|Quito]] and its valleys, with farming of [[e:maize|maize]] and [[e:potato|potatoes]] and markets where goods from the coast and [[e:amazon|Amazon]] were traded. [[e:juan-de-velasco|Velasco]]'s account of a centralised kingdom with a line of Shyri kings has no support from earlier chronicles and is widely regarded as legend, though it became a cornerstone of Ecuadorian national identity.
quitu-cara.e: The [[e:quito|Quito]] region fell to the [[e:inca-empire|Incas]] in the late 15th century and became their northern capital under [[e:huayna-capac|Huayna Capac]]. After [[e:atahualpa|Atahualpa's]] capture, the Inca general Rumiñahui held Quito until the Spanish took it in 1534.

qaraqushs-tripolitania.t: The freebooting domain of Sharaf al-Din Qaraqush, an Ayyubid mamluk who carved out power in Tripolitania and southern Ifriqiya against the Almohads.
qaraqushs-tripolitania.o: [[e:sharaf-al-din-qaraqush|Qaraqush]], an Armenian mamluk in the service of [[e:taqi-al-din-umar|Taqi al-Din]], nephew of [[e:saladin|Saladin]], led Turkish and [[e:oghuz-turks|Ghuzz]] soldiers west from [[e:egypt|Egypt]] around 1172. Exploiting [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohad]] weakness east of [[e:tunis|Tunis]], he gathered support from Arab tribes and took towns in [[s:tripolitania|Tripolitania]], the [[e:nafusa-mountains|Jabal Nafusa]] and the region of [[e:gabes|Gabès]], acting as an adventurer more than as an agent of the [[s:ayyubid-empire|Ayyubid Empire]].
qaraqushs-tripolitania.r: His power rested on a mobile army of Turkish soldiers and [[e:bedouin|Bedouin]] allies rather than settled institutions. He allied at times with the [[s:banu-ghaniya-of-ifriqiya|Banu Ghaniya of Ifriqiya]] against the [[s:almohad-caliphate|Almohad Caliphate]], and the two sides' campaigns ravaged southern [[e:tunisia|Tunisia]] and [[s:tripolitania|Tripolitania]]. Little is known of any administration beyond tribute and plunder.
qaraqushs-tripolitania.e: [[e:sharaf-al-din-qaraqush|Qaraqush]] lost ground to [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohad]] counter-attacks and then quarrelled with his [[s:banu-ghaniya-of-ifriqiya|Banu Ghaniya]] allies. [[e:yahya-ibn-ghaniya|Yahya ibn Ghaniya]] captured and killed him around 1212 in the oases of the [[s:sultanate-of-fezzan|Fezzan]] region, and his followers dispersed.

quba-khanate.t: A khanate in north-eastern Azerbaijan whose ruler Fatali Khan united much of the eastern Caucasus in the late 18th century.
quba-khanate.o: The khanate grew out of the [[e:quba|Quba]] district on the Caspian slope of the [[e:caucasus|Caucasus]]. Its rulers, from a local family, were recognised by the [[s:safavid-empire|Safavid Empire]] in 1726 and by [[e:nader-shah|Nader Shah]], and after Nader's death in 1747 [[e:husayn-ali-khan-of-quba|Husayn Ali Khan]] ruled as an effectively independent khan from his new town of Quba.
quba-khanate.r: [[e:fatali-khan-of-quba|Fatali Khan]], who ruled from 1758, conquered the [[s:derbent-khanate|Derbent Khanate]] in 1765, dominated the [[s:baku-khanate|Baku Khanate]] and the [[s:javad-khanate|Javad Khanate]] and took [[e:shamakhi|Shamakhi]], creating the largest state in the eastern [[e:caucasus|Caucasus]]. He built a strong administration and army and negotiated with [[e:catherine-the-great|Catherine the Great]]. The khanate lived from farming, carpets, [[e:silk|silk]] and Caspian trade.
quba-khanate.e: After [[e:fatali-khan-of-quba|Fatali Khan]]'s death in 1789, his union fell apart. His son [[e:sheikh-ali-khan-of-quba|Sheikh Ali Khan]] resisted the Russian advance, but in 1806 the [[s:russian-empire|Russian Empire]] occupied [[e:quba|Quba]] and [[e:derbent|Derbent]] and later abolished the khanate.

qarinvand-dynasty.t: A branch of the great Parthian noble house of Karen that ruled the mountains of Tabaristan for three centuries, until its last prince Mazyar rebelled against the Abbasids.
qarinvand-dynasty.o: The [[e:house-of-karen|Karen]] were one of the seven great noble houses of Parthian and Sasanian [[e:iran|Iran]]. According to [[e:ibn-isfandiyar|Ibn Isfandiyar's]] history of [[e:tabaristan|Tabaristan]], [[e:khosrow-i|Khosrow I]] granted the descendants of [[e:sukhra|Sukhra]] land in the mountains of Tabaristan around 550, after their service against the [[s:hephthalite-empire|Hephthalites]]. The family held the highland district later called the 'Mountains of Qarin'.
qarinvand-dynasty.r: The Qarinvandids were local princes with the Persian title ispahbad or similar, ruling a Zoroastrian peasant society in the [[e:alborz|Alborz]] forests and valleys. After the Arab conquest they held out alongside the [[s:dabuyid-dynasty|Dabuyid dynasty]] and the [[s:bavand-dynasty|Bavand dynasty]], paying tribute but keeping their faith. [[e:vandad-hormozd|Vandad Hormozd]] led a revolt against the [[s:abbasid-caliphate|Abbasid Caliphate]] in the 780s, and his son Qarin continued the family's power.
qarinvand-dynasty.e: [[e:mazyar|Mazyar ibn Qarin]] converted to [[e:islam|Islam]] and served [[e:al-mamun|al-Ma'mun]], but rebelled against the [[e:caliphate|caliph]] [[e:al-mutasim|al-Mu'tasim]] and the [[s:tahirid-dynasty|Tahirid dynasty]] in 839. He was captured and executed in [[e:samarra|Samarra]] in 840, ending the dynasty.
